package_info.package_versions: N/A (malware family, not a package version)
package_info.why_malicious: The SNOWLIGHT malware family is designed for remote access, command execution, and credential theft on Linux systems. It is deployed post-exploitation via exploitation of public-facing application vulnerabilities (e.g., F5 BIG-IP, ScreenConnect), and exhibits behaviors such as obfuscation, file deletion, privilege escalation, and command-and-control communication with attacker infrastructure.

execution_context.file_location: Deployed Linux ELF binary (SNOWLIGHT sample, e.g., MD5: 0951109dd1be0d84a33d52c135ba9c97)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code performs XOR-based obfuscation/decoding of payloads in memory, enabling the decryption and execution of additional malicious code.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of custom XOR routines for in-memory decoding is a common malware technique to evade static detection and hinder analysis.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate binaries rarely use custom XOR loops to decode large code sections or payloads at runtime, especially in system utilities.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate software may use XOR for simple obfuscation of configuration data, but not for large-scale code decryption.
key_indicators: Custom XOR loop in code section

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: { BA 01 00 00 00 BE 3B 0B 40 00 BF 3F 01 00 00 E8 8C FE FF FF }
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code invokes the memfd_create syscall to create an anonymous, in-memory file descriptor, then writes and executes additional payloads from memory, enabling fileless execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The use of memfd_create for in-memory, fileless payload execution is a known malware anti-forensics and evasion technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal applications rarely use memfd_create for executable payloads; this is a hallmark of advanced malware.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some container runtimes or advanced system tools may use memfd_create for legitimate in-memory operations, but not for arbitrary code execution.

execution_context.file_location: Deployed Linux ELF binary (GOREVERSE sample, e.g., MD5: 5c175ea3664279d6c0c2609844de6949)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
‘–[foreground|fingerprint|proxy|process_name] -d|–destination <server_address>’
‘-d or –destination Server connect back address (can be baked in)’
‘–foreground Causes the client to run without forking to background’
‘–fingerprint Server public key SHA256 hex fingerprint for auth’
‘–proxy Location of HTTP connect proxy to use’
‘–process_name Process name shown in tasklist/process list’
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code parses command-line arguments to configure a reverse shell client, which connects back to a specified C2 server, optionally using a proxy, and can masquerade its process name.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Reverse shell clients that connect to attacker-controlled infrastructure and allow process name masquerading are classic indicators of backdoor malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not provide reverse shell functionality or allow arbitrary process name spoofing for evasion.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Penetration testing tools may use similar options, but are not present in production environments.
key_indicators: Destination server address baked into binary

attack_chain.action: Attacker exploits public-facing application vulnerabilities (F5 BIG-IP CVE-2023-46747 or ScreenConnect CVE-2024-1709) to gain initial access.
Attacker uploads and executes SNOWLIGHT or GOREVERSE malware on the compromised system.
Malware decodes and executes additional payloads in memory, establishes reverse shell connections to attacker C2 infrastructure, and enables remote command execution.
attack_chain.leads_to: Credential theft, lateral movement, and further post-exploitation

attack_chain.action: Malware may perform credential theft (e.g., /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow), system discovery, and anti-forensics (file deletion, process masquerading).

behavioral_signatures: Use of XOR-based in-memory decoding routines in Linux ELF binaries
Use of memfd_create syscall for fileless payload execution
Reverse shell connections to hardcoded or attacker-controlled C2 addresses
Command-line arguments enabling reverse shell or proxy configuration
file_indicators: Linux ELF binaries with MD5 hashes: 0951109dd1be0d84a33d52c135ba9c97, c867881c56698f938b4e8edafe76a09b, df4603548b10211f0aa77d0e9a172438, 0ba435460fb7622344eec28063274b8a, a78bf3d16349eba86719539ee8ef562d
Presence of binaries named or containing 'goreverse', 'snowlight', or similar
Unusual binaries in /tmp, /dev/shm, or other writable directories
network_indicators: Non-application layer protocol traffic (custom C2, reverse shell)
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for execution of unknown or suspicious Linux ELF binaries, especially those using XOR-based decoding or memfd_create for in-memory execution. Detect outbound connections to known C2 infrastructure and monitor for reverse shell behavior (unexpected outbound connections, process name spoofing, or command-line arguments indicating reverse shell configuration). Use YARA rules provided by Mandiant to scan for known malware families (SNOWLIGHT, GOREVERSE) and correlate with file hashes and network indicators.
